latin.515: Sed, ut omnis expugnetur pertinacia, loco introiit pone imputatum est, vide quam belle procedet Apostoli oratio, per unum hominem peccatum imputatum est mundo, & per peccatum mors. Num imputata est mors? num imputata est per peccatum? num peccatum est imputatum per Adamum? Nonne ridiculum, quantum in ipsis est, qui sic contra me disputant, faciunt Apostolum?
latin.516: GAR. 5. Itaque quamquam singularis actio, ratione substantiae suae non potest dici introire in alium, tamen ratione reatus introire recte dicitur, quatenus propter actionem illam alius reus habetur, adeoque poenis subiacet.
latin.517: PLAC. Atqui 1. aliud est actio, aliud reatus. Illa est actio, haec relatio, illa transit, hoc manet. Num igitur si reatus recte dicitur introire, recte etiam dicitur introire actio? Num quicquid dicitur de reatu, dici etiam potest de actione? Num actio est relatio? num manet postquam actio transiit? num sequitur actionem? 2. Aliud est propter actionem reum haberi, aliud reatum actionis introire in aliquem: illud externam tantum denominationem significat, hoc aliquid importat amplius. Imo ipse reatus, cum sit relatio, introire dici non potest, nisi aut ratione fundamenti, hoc est, peccati sive sit actio, sive habitus, aut termini, hoc est, poenae, tantum abest ut ratione reatus actio dici possit in alium introire.
latin.518: GAR. 6. Denique imputatio peccati, est illa quidem actio Dei, a Deo tanquam judice profecta, sed in homines tendens, tanquam in terminum, & eo respectu in hominem intrans aut veniens, propter effectus quos in ipso producit, id est, propter poenas quibus eum afficit. Sic maledictio est actio Dei Gen. XII. 3. Malach. 2. 2. Et tamen intrare dicitur in homines aliquos Psal. CIX. 18. Maledictio ingredietur, velut aqua, intra eum, & velut oleum in ossa eius. Quod autem imputatio peccati sit actio Dei intra Deum manens Theologi vix concedant, qui cum Dei actiones distinguere soleant in immanentes & transeuntes; immanentes eas vocant, quae in ipso Deo terminantur, ut intellectionem, & volitionem, qua seipsum intelligit & diligit: transeuntes, quae terminantur in creaturas, quales sunt actiones divinae providentiae. Sed haec aliis disceptanda relinquo.
latin.519: PLAC. Quis unquam negavit Dei actiones alias esse immanentes, alias transeuntes; illas in Deo, has in creaturis esse? Et quis nescit in hoc posteriore genere ponendam esse maledictionem quae est actio Dei? Quanquam per maledictionem Ps. CIX. 18. non significatur actio, sed effectum potius Dei irati, nempe miseria, infortunium, malum poenae. Vult Propheta huiusmodi hominem omnibus malis corporalibus & spiritualibus omni ex parte induti & penetrari. Itaque praecessit, optavit ut maledictio eveniret ei, & sequitur, Hoc esto praemium adversantium mihi &c. Quid autem hoc ad rem, qua de agimus, facit? Quaeritur quo sensu dixerit Apostolus per unum hominem peccatum introiisse in mundum, id est, in homines? Dicis per peccatum intelligendam esse actionem Adami. Quaero, quomodo actio Adami, quae diu antequam ulli alii homines essent, fuerat praeterita ac esse desierat, dici potuit in omnes homines introiisse? Dicis introiisse imputatione. Repono, imputationem illam non esse actionem unius illius hominis, sed solius Dei. Non igitur per unum hominem, sed per Deum peccatum introiisse in omnes homines: quo nihil dici potest absurdius.
latin.520: Repono etiam, non fieri imputatione illa ut peccatum actuale, seu actio illa praeterita Adami, unquam intra nos fuerit, aut esse possit. Repono denique imputationem, aut esse actionem mentis seu iudicii divini reputantis nos esse reos actionis illius Adamicae, aut illius divini iudicii declarationem lata sententia sermone externo, aut poenae inflictionem.

pass_a.515: But to storm all obstinacy: put imputatum est in place of introiit, and see how finely the Apostle's speech proceeds—'through one man sin was imputed to the world, and through sin death.' Was death imputed? Imputed through sin? Was sin imputed through Adam? Do not those who dispute me so make the Apostle, as far as in them lies, ridiculous?
pass_a.516: GAR 5: A one-off deed cannot, as substance, be said to walk into another man; yet by reatus it may—because of that deed he is held guilty and so under penalties.
pass_a.517: PLAC: But (1) action is one thing, reatus another—deed versus relation; the deed passes, the relation remains. If reatus is rightly said to enter, is the action too? Whatever is said of reatus—said of the action? Is action a relation? Does it remain after the deed passed? Does it follow the deed? (2) To be held guilty because of an action is one thing; for the action's reatus to enter someone is another—the first is only an external name, the second imports more. Indeed reatus itself, being a relation, cannot be said to enter except by its foundation (sin as act or habit) or its term (penalty)—so far is it from the action entering another by reatus.
pass_a.518: GAR 6: Finally sin's imputation is God's action, proceeding from God as judge, yet tending into humans as its term—and in that respect entering or coming into a human by the effects it produces in him, the penalties it afflicts him with. So curse is God's action (Gen 12:3; Mal 2:2), yet is said to enter some (Ps 109:18): 'the curse shall enter like water into him, and like oil into his bones.' That imputation is an action remaining only inside God theologians hardly grant, who divide God's acts into immanent (terminating in God—intellection, volition) and transeunt (terminating in creatures—providence). But I leave that to others.
pass_a.519: PLAC: Who ever denied some divine acts are immanent, some transeunt—those in God, these in creatures? And who does not know curse as God's act belongs to the latter? Yet in Ps 109:18 'curse' means not the act but rather the effect of an angry God—misery, misfortune, the evil of penalty. The prophet wants such a man clothed and pierced every way with all bodily and spiritual evils. So he first wished the curse to befall him, then 'let this be the reward of my adversaries,' etc. What does that do for our question? In what sense did Paul say sin entered the world through one man—into humans? You say sin = Adam's action. How could that action, long past and ceased before any other humans were, be said to have entered into all? You say by imputation. I reply: that imputation is not the action of that one man but of God alone. So not through one man but through God sin entered all—than which nothing more absurd can be said.
pass_a.520: I reply also that by that imputation Adam's past actual never was, nor can be, inside us. I reply finally that imputation is either (a) an act of the divine mind/judgment reckoning us guilty of that Adamic deed, or (b) a declaration of that judgment by external sentence, or (c) the infliction of penalty. Tip before working those three.

515: But, that every obstinacy may be stormed, in place of introiit put imputatum est, see how finely the Apostle's speech will proceed: through one man sin was imputed to the world, and through sin death. Was death imputed? Was it imputed through sin? Was sin imputed through Adam? Do they not make the Apostle ridiculous, as far as in them lies, who so dispute against me?
516: GAR. 5. And so although a singular action, by reason of its substance, cannot be said to enter into another, yet by reason of reatus it is rightly said to enter, insofar as because of that action another is held guilty, and so lies under penalties.
517: PLAC. But 1. action is one thing, reatus another. That is an action, this a relation, that passes, this remains. Is it then, if reatus is rightly said to enter, rightly also said that the action enters? Can whatever is said of reatus also be said of the action? Is action a relation? Does it remain after the action has passed? Does it follow the action? 2. It is one thing to be held guilty because of an action, another for the reatus of the action to enter into someone: that signifies only an external denomination, this imports something more. Nay the reatus itself, since it is a relation, cannot be said to enter, except either by reason of the foundation, that is, of sin whether it be action or habit, or of the term, that is, of penalty, so far is it from it that by reason of reatus the action can be said to enter into another.
518: GAR. 6. Finally the imputation of sin is indeed that action of God, proceeding from God as judge, but tending into humans, as into a term, and in that respect entering or coming into a human, because of the effects which it produces in him, that is, because of the penalties with which it afflicts him. So curse is an action of God Gen. XII. 3. Malachi 2. 2. And yet it is said to enter into some humans Psalm 109. 18. The curse shall enter, like water, within him, and like oil into his bones. But that the imputation of sin is an action of God remaining inside God theologians hardly grant, who are accustomed to distinguish God's actions into immanent and transeunt; they call immanent those which terminate in God himself, as intellection, and volition, by which he understands and loves himself: transeunt, those which terminate in creatures, such as the actions of divine providence. But these I leave to be disputed by others.
519: PLAC. Who ever denied that God's actions are some immanent, some transeunt; those in God, these in creatures? And who does not know that into this latter kind must be placed the curse which is an action of God? Although by the curse in Psalm 109. 18. is not signified the action, but rather the effect of an angry God, namely misery, misfortune, the evil of penalty. The Prophet wants a man of this kind to be clothed and penetrated on every side with all bodily and spiritual evils. And so it preceded, he wished that the curse would befall him, and there follows, Let this be the reward of those opposing me, etc. But what does this do for the matter we are treating? It is asked in what sense the Apostle said that through one man sin entered into the world, that is, into humans? You say that by sin Adam's action must be understood. I ask, how could Adam's action, which long before any other humans were, had been past and had ceased to be, be said to have entered into all humans? You say it entered by imputation. I reply, that imputation is not the action of that one man, but of God alone. Not therefore through one man, but through God, did sin enter into all humans: than which nothing more absurd can be said.
520: I reply also, that by that imputation it does not come about that the actual sin, or that past action of Adam, ever was inside us, or can be. I reply finally that imputation is either an action of the mind or of the divine judgment reckoning us to be guilty of that Adamic action, or a declaration of that divine judgment by a sentence passed in external speech, or the infliction of penalty.
